22	                                      Background: Hamstring strain injuries are one of the most prevalent injuries in football (soccer). We examined the
23	                                      influence of accumulated match-play exposure on the occurrence of hamstring strain injury in professional football from 2
24	                                      teams (Spanish 1st Division, LaLiga) over 3 seasons, and determined specific cut-off points as indicators of injury risk.
25	                                      Hypothesis: Overloaded players would be more likely to sustain a hamstring injury.
26	                                      Study Design: Prospective, controlled, observational study.
27	                                      Level of Evidence: Level 2b.
28	                                      Methods: Playing time, total running distance, and high-speed running (>24 km/h) distance during official matches of
29	                                      players that sustained a hamstring injury were compared with uninjured, paired controls. Cumulative playing time and
30	                                      running performance of 4 matches before the injury was computed. Relative risk (RR) of injury occurrence was estimated
31	                                      by generalized estimating equations. Diagnostic accuracy was determined by receiver operating characteristics and the area
32	                                      under the curve.
33	                                      Results: Thirty-seven hamstring strain injuries occurred, representing 23 ± 18 absence days per injury. Thirty-seven controls
34	                                      (uninjured players) were used as comparators. Low match-play exposures during 1 and 2 matches before injury were likely
35	                                      to explain injury occurrence (RR: 14-53%; P < 0.01). Metrics from the match before the hamstring muscle strain demonstrated
36	                                      the best accuracy to predict injury occurrence: high-speed running distance ≤328 m (sensitivity, 64%; specificity, 84%),
37	                                      playing time ≤64 min (sensitivity, 36%; specificity, 97%), and running distance ≤5.8 km (sensitivity, 39%; specificity, 97%).
38	                                      Conclusion: Relatively reduced competitive exposure in the previous 2 matches was associated with higher hamstring
39	                                      injury risk in professional football players.
40	                                      Clinical Relevance: Screening simple metrics such as the accumulated match exposure during official matches and
41	                                      considering specific cut-off points for some running variables may be good indicators of injury risk and may assist in better
42	                                      individual injury management in professional soccer players.
43	                                      Keywords: external workload; injury prevention; musculoskeletal; soccer; team sports

                                      Reduced Match Exposure in the Previous
                                      2 Matches Accounts for Hamstring
                                      Muscle Injury Incidence in Professional
                                      Football Players
                                      Víctor Moreno-Pérez, PhD,†‡ Juan Del Coso, PhD,§ Roberto López-Del Campo, PhD,||
                                      Ricardo Resta, PhD,|| José Romero-Sangüesa, MSc,¶ Javier Courel-Ibáñez, PhD,*#
                                      and Alberto Méndez-Villanueva, PhD**


                                      Background: Hamstring strain injuries are one of the most prevalent injuries in football (soccer). We examined the
                                      influence of accumulated match-play exposure on the occurrence of hamstring strain injury in professional football from 2
                                      teams (Spanish 1st Division, LaLiga) over 3 seasons, and determined specific cut-off points as indicators of injury risk.
                                      Hypothesis: Overloaded players would be more likely to sustain a hamstring injury.
                                      Study Design: Prospective, controlled, observational study.
                                      Level of Evidence: Level 2b.
                                      Methods: Playing time, total running distance, and high-speed running (>24 km/h) distance during official matches of
                                      players that sustained a hamstring injury were compared with uninjured, paired controls. Cumulative playing time and
                                      running performance of 4 matches before the injury was computed. Relative risk (RR) of injury occurrence was estimated
                                      by generalized estimating equations. Diagnostic accuracy was determined by receiver operating characteristics and the area
                                      under the curve.
                                      Results: Thirty-seven hamstring strain injuries occurred, representing 23 ± 18 absence days per injury. Thirty-seven controls
                                      (uninjured players) were used as comparators. Low match-play exposures during 1 and 2 matches before injury were likely
                                      to explain injury occurrence (RR: 14-53%; P < 0.01). Metrics from the match before the hamstring muscle strain demonstrated
                                      the best accuracy to predict injury occurrence: high-speed running distance ≤328 m (sensitivity, 64%; specificity, 84%),
                                      playing time ≤64 min (sensitivity, 36%; specificity, 97%), and running distance ≤5.8 km (sensitivity, 39%; specificity, 97%).
                                      Conclusion: Relatively reduced competitive exposure in the previous 2 matches was associated with higher hamstring
                                      injury risk in professional football players.
                                      Clinical Relevance: Screening simple metrics such as the accumulated match exposure during official matches and
                                      considering specific cut-off points for some running variables may be good indicators of injury risk and may assist in better
                                      individual injury management in professional soccer players.
                                      Keywords: external workload; injury prevention; musculoskeletal; soccer; team sports

1	                                                                                    Open Access Journal of Sports Medicine
2	
3	                                                                                        Open Access Full Text Article
4	                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  REVIEW
5	
6	                                                                                    Reference Values for Hydration Biomarkers:
7	                                                                                    Optimizing Athletic Performance and Recovery
8	                                                                                    Lawrence E Armstrong 1 , Rebecca L Stearns 1 , Robert A Huggins 1 , Yasuki Sekiguchi 2 ,
9	                                                                                    April J Mershon 3 , Douglas J Casa 1
10	
11	
12	
13	
14	Open Access Journal of Sports Medicine downloaded from https://www.dovepress.com/
15	                                                                                    1
16	                                                                                    Department of Kinesiology, Korey Stringer Institute, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, 06269-1110, USA; 2Department of Kinesiology & Sport
17	                                                                                    Management, Sports Performance Laboratory, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, 79409, USA; 3Private Consultant, Williamsburg, VA, 23188, USA
18	
19	                                                                                    Correspondence: Lawrence E Armstrong, Email lawrence.armstrong@uconn.edu
20	
21	
22	                                                                                    Abstract: The negative effects of dehydration or overhydration on exercise performance and health are widely recognized. However,
23	                                                                                    the interindividual variability of fluid imbalances among athletes and across various sports is large, due to the complex interactions of
24	                                                                                    physiological, environmental, and sport-specific factors. Such complexity not only makes it difficult to predict fluid needs prior to
25	                                                                                    competition or training sessions, but also supports the creation of an individualized hydration plan (IHP) for each athlete.
26	                                                                                    Measurements of valid, field-expedient biomarkers such as body mass change, urine concentration, and thirst enable ongoing
27	                                                                                    monitoring of an athlete’s hydration state and are integral components of an IHP. Unfortunately, no extensive repository of sport-
28	                                                                                    relevant hydration biomarker data exists. Therefore, this narrative review presents a novel inventory of pre- and post-exercise reference
29	
30	
31	
32	
33	                              For personal use only.
34	                                                                                    values for body mass change, urine specific gravity, and subjective rating of thirst. These reference values were identified via
35	                                                                                    electronic database searches that discovered field studies of competitive events, weight category sports, training sessions, and routine
36	                                                                                    daily activities. We propose that comparing an athlete’s real-time body mass change, urine specific gravity, and thirst rating to
37	                                                                                    previously published reference values will clarify the extent of dehydration or overhydration, guide rehydration efforts, and optimize
38	                                                                                    subsequent exercise performance, recovery, and health.
39	                                                                                    Keywords: urine specific gravity, thirst, runner, cyclist, swimmer, triathlete
40	
41	
42	
43	                                                                                    Introduction
44	                                                                                    Deficits of total body water are relevant to all athletes because substantial fluid losses degrade competitive sport
45	                                                                                    performance1–4 and increase the risk of exertional heat illnesses, especially heat exhaustion.5–9 Dehydration potentiates
46	                                                                                    hyperthermia, increases cardiovascular strain, and elevates perceived exertion. Specifically, a body mass loss of 3–4%
47	                                                                                    induced by dehydration may decrease muscular strength by 2%, muscular power by 3%, and high-intensity endurance
48	                                                                                    exercise by 10%.1,10 As the body water deficit increases (ie, due to unreplaced fluid losses during outdoor competition,
49	                                                                                    training sessions, “making weight” in combat sports, or routine daily activities), both detrimental physiological effects
50	                                                                                    (ie, which often influence exercise) and clinical signs and symptoms proliferate.11–13
51	                                                                                        The following documented scenarios illustrate the wide range of fluid deficits that are experienced by athletes in
52	                                                                                    various team and individual sports. During hot summer months, collegiate American football linemen can lose 4–6 kg of
53	                                                                                    body water during a single summer practice session,5 and the sweat rates of tennis players and marathon runners during
54	                                                                                    competition reach extremes of 3.4 and 3.7 L/h, respectively.14,15 In moderate or cool environments, ultraendurance
55	                                                                                    athletes can experience extreme body water losses (7.8–8.5 kg, 11–12% of body mass) when competing in
56	                                                                                    a 12.3 h Ironman triathlon event.16 During 1.5–2.5 h training sessions across a variety of sports (eg, European soccer,
57	                                                                                    American football, tennis, cross country), body mass deficits typically range from 0.5–3.2% when fluids are readily
58	                                                                                    available.17–20 Other athletes purposefully dehydrate to qualify for lower weight classes (eg, wrestling, martial arts); this
59	                                                                                    regimen can result in body water losses of 3–5%.21,22 Even on days that are void of training or competition, it is possible
60	                                                                                    for healthy young adults to incur a 2.1% body mass loss during a single day of routine activities if no fluid is consumed.23
61	
62	                                                                                                                               Open Access Journal of Sports Medicine 2025:16 31–50                                                                                                                                  31
63	                                                                                    Received: 26 November 2024                                       © 2025 Armstrong et al. This work is published and licensed by Dove Medical Press Limited. The full terms of this license are available at https://www.dovepress.com/

67	                                    Armstrong et al
68	
69	
70	                                       At the opposite end of the hydration continuum, some endurance athletes consume a large volume of fluid that greatly
71	                                   exceeds the volume of fluid which he/she lost as sweat. Because sodium is lost in sweat, the outcomes are dilution of body
72	                                   fluids and reduced blood concentration of sodium.24 This phenomenon is appropriately named exertional hyponatremia or
73	                                   water intoxication. Not only does exertional hyponatremia degrade exercise performance (eg, due to undue fatigue), but severe
74	                                   cases may result in coma, pulmonary edema, cerebral edema, or death.4 The prominent signs and symptoms include dilute
75	                                   urine, swollen hands, disorientation, nausea, vomiting, skeletal muscle twitching, and grand mal seizure.25 Documented cases
76	                                   of symptomatic exertional hyponatremia26,27 have shown that fluid volumes of 10.3–14.7 L were consumed during exercise
77	                                   lasting 4–10 h. However, exertional hyponatremia has also been verified among non-endurance athletes,4,24 soldiers,28 and
78	                                   individuals who erroneously believed that excessive water intake was beneficial to performance or health.26 To reduce the risk
79	                                   of exertional hyponatremia, athletes are advised to gain no weight during exercise (ie, signifying fluid retention), and use
80	                                   a digital floor scale before and after exercise to confirm body weight change.3
81	                                       The aforementioned large range of body water changes, coupled with the dynamic/complex physiological effector
82	                                   responses that occur when the brain senses altered body water volume or concentration,29–33 represents great complexity
83	                                   that makes it difficult (ie, for clinicians, physiologists, athletes, or coaches) to accurately predict in advance the fluid
84	                                   deficit or excess which any athlete might experience during training or competition. This complexity explains, in part,
85	                                   why no single hydration biomarker allows a conclusive clinical diagnosis of dehydration for all athletes in all sport
86	                                   scenarios.34–39 Thus, we recommend creating an individualized hydration plan (IHP) for each athlete which incorporates
87	                                   multiple biomarkers, in agreement with numerous investigators and professional organizations.3,4,27,40–43 Specifically, we
88	                                   recommend three hydration indices which are inexpensive, valid, and require minimal technical expertise: body mass
89	                                   change, urine specific gravity, and rating of thirst. This approach provides athletes with data that is unique in the existing
90	                                   literature because most publications4,44–50 provide only a single hydration biomarker measurement (eg, urine specific
91	                                   gravity of 1.020) or a narrow range of values (eg, body mass loss of 3–4%) for all athletes, to indicate the threshold of
92	                                   dehydration’s detrimental effects. Using only one biomarker to assess hydration state is inferior, however, because (a)
93	                                   interindividual variability of fluid–electrolyte imbalances is large and is influenced by many factors;31,51–54 and (b)
94	                                   research studies31,55 have determined that combining two or three hydration indices (ie, body mass change, urine
95	                                   concentration, and thirst rating) improves the likelihood of distinguishing hypohydration from euhydration (ie, an optimal
96	                                   body water balance without underhydration or overhydration). In addition, our three criterion biomarker approach
97	                                   contributes importantly to the literature because no inventory of hydration biomarker data exists to guide interpretation
98	                                   of the unique body water changes (ie, deficits or excesses) which athletes experience in various sports.
99	                                       Therefore, the purpose of this review is to provide reference values for three field expedient biomarkers: body mass
100	                                   change, urine specific gravity, and rating of thirst. We have assembled a novel inventory of reference values for these
101	                                   three hydration biomarkers from field studies that involved outdoor competitions, training sessions, “making weight” in
102	                                   combat sports, and performing routine daily activities with no exercise. This collection of reference values is intended for
103	                                   use by clinicians, athletes, coaches, and physiologists, (a) as one of multiple resources that can be utilized to create and
104	                                   evaluate IHP for athletes and (b) to interpret hydration status before physical training or competition, post-exercise
105	                                   dehydration or excess fluid intake/retention, rehydration that optimizes recovery and health, and hydration status during
106	                                   routine daily activities.
107	
108	                                   Search Methods
109	                                   Manual searches for relevant articles were performed using advanced search operators (eg, “and”, “or”, “not”). These
110	                                   searches focused on field studies that incorporated measurements of three human hydration biomarkers: body mass, urine
111	                                   specific gravity, and subjective ratings of thirst. Search inclusion criteria included English language, full-text, peer-
112	                                   reviewed articles with adult test participants, and availability through May 1, 2024. These searches were performed in the
113	                                   PubMed and Google Scholar databases; they employed numerous combinations of the following keywords, during
114	                                   separate explorations of the title/abstract and all text fields: “athlete”, “athletic”, “sports”, “hydration”, “hydrate”,
115	                                   “hydrated”, “hydrates”, “hydrating”, “biomarker”, “biomarkers”, “index”, “indexes”, “indices”, “indicators”, “urine
116	                                   specific gravity”, “thirst”, “body mass”, and “body weight”. These online searches acknowledged that the authors of
117	                                   hydration-relevant articles rarely distinguish the term “body mass” from “body weight”.
118	
119	
120	                                   32        https://doi.org/10.2147/OAJSM.S508656                                      Open Access Journal of Sports Medicine 2025:16
121	
122	
123	
124	Powered by TCPDF (www.tcpdf.org)
125	                                                                                                                                                                    Armstrong et al
126	
127	
128	                                       Using these search terms within PubMed and Google Scholar databases, initially 3,224 articles were identified as
129	                                   potentially relevant (Figure 1). After duplicate records were removed, we reviewed titles and abstracts (ie, seeking
130	                                   studies that reported body mass change, urine specific gravity, and a subjective thirst rating as hydration indices) to
131	                                   identify potentially appropriate full-length articles which should be assessed further. Also, we performed manual searches
132	                                   of the reference lists in these relevant articles, as well as the bibliographies found in germane systematic reviews and
133	                                   meta-analyses. Finally, we investigated full text (.pdf) versions of 385 articles to ascertain if they met our inclusion
134	                                   criteria. Figure 1 illustrates the steps in this selection process.
135	
136	
137	                                   Results
138	                                   Using the keywords, inclusion criteria, and methods described above, we accepted 16 articles for analysis within the
139	                                   present review. All of these 16 articles measured body mass with a floor scale and urine specific gravity with a handheld
140	                                   refractometer; subjective ratings of thirst were measured using one of the two methods (eg, category scale or visual
141	                                   analog scale) described in footnotes b and e of Table 1. Thus, the following tables present measurements of only body
142	                                   weight change, urine specific gravity, and subjective rating of thirst during a variety of athletic and routine daily
143	                                   activities. For example, Table 1 presents reference values which can be utilized by clinicians, coaches, physiologists,
144	                                   and athletes to develop an IHP for use during outdoor athletic competitions and training sessions.
145	                                       Table 2 focuses on combat sport (ie, wrestling, boxing, judo) athletes who attempt rapid body mass loss to qualify for
146	                                   a weight class. Although our extensive literature search identified only a few studies of this type, values are provided for
147	                                   both pre- and post-weigh-in. Table 3 describes the changes of body mass, urine specific gravity, and subjective thirst ratings
148	                                   of two men who developed exertional hyponatremia during a 164-km summer ultraendurance cycling event.27 In column 4,
149	                                   mean (± SD) values are presented for a comparison group of 31 normonatremic cyclists who participated in the same event.
150	                                       In Table 1 and 2, the relationship between average body mass change and urine specific gravity (r = 0.50, p = 0.013), as well
151	                                   as the relationship between average body mass change and rating of thirst (r = 0.68, p = 0.001), were significantly correlated.
152	                                       Table 4 and 5 describe our three criterion hydration biomarkers, as they were measured during the routine daily
153	                                   activities of representative, healthy young adults. The test participants in these field studies23,68–70 were nonathletes who
154	                                   either performed recreational exercise (Table 4) or refrained from exercise (Table 5). The experimental design of the
155	                                   former study69,70 allowed a comparison of the average differences between morning and afternoon measurements. The
156	                                   latter field study (Table 5) illustrates hydration biomarker perturbations that resulted from a 24-h period of water

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  REVIEW

                                                                                    Reference Values for Hydration Biomarkers:
                                                                                    Optimizing Athletic Performance and Recovery
                                                                                    Lawrence E Armstrong 1 , Rebecca L Stearns 1 , Robert A Huggins 1 , Yasuki Sekiguchi 2 ,
                                                                                    April J Mershon 3 , Douglas J Casa 1




Open Access Journal of Sports Medicine downloaded from https://www.dovepress.com/
                                                                                    1
                                                                                    Department of Kinesiology, Korey Stringer Institute, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, 06269-1110, USA; 2Department of Kinesiology & Sport
                                                                                    Management, Sports Performance Laboratory, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, 79409, USA; 3Private Consultant, Williamsburg, VA, 23188, USA

                                                                                    Correspondence: Lawrence E Armstrong, Email lawrence.armstrong@uconn.edu


                                                                                    Abstract: The negative effects of dehydration or overhydration on exercise performance and health are widely recognized. However,
                                                                                    the interindividual variability of fluid imbalances among athletes and across various sports is large, due to the complex interactions of
                                                                                    physiological, environmental, and sport-specific factors. Such complexity not only makes it difficult to predict fluid needs prior to
                                                                                    competition or training sessions, but also supports the creation of an individualized hydration plan (IHP) for each athlete.
                                                                                    Measurements of valid, field-expedient biomarkers such as body mass change, urine concentration, and thirst enable ongoing
                                                                                    monitoring of an athlete’s hydration state and are integral components of an IHP. Unfortunately, no extensive repository of sport-
                                                                                    relevant hydration biomarker data exists. Therefore, this narrative review presents a novel inventory of pre- and post-exercise reference




                              For personal use only.
                                                                                    values for body mass change, urine specific gravity, and subjective rating of thirst. These reference values were identified via
                                                                                    electronic database searches that discovered field studies of competitive events, weight category sports, training sessions, and routine
                                                                                    daily activities. We propose that comparing an athlete’s real-time body mass change, urine specific gravity, and thirst rating to
                                                                                    previously published reference values will clarify the extent of dehydration or overhydration, guide rehydration efforts, and optimize
                                                                                    subsequent exercise performance, recovery, and health.
                                                                                    Keywords: urine specific gravity, thirst, runner, cyclist, swimmer, triathlete



                                                                                    Introduction
                                                                                    Deficits of total body water are relevant to all athletes because substantial fluid losses degrade competitive sport
                                                                                    performance1–4 and increase the risk of exertional heat illnesses, especially heat exhaustion.5–9 Dehydration potentiates
                                                                                    hyperthermia, increases cardiovascular strain, and elevates perceived exertion. Specifically, a body mass loss of 3–4%
                                                                                    induced by dehydration may decrease muscular strength by 2%, muscular power by 3%, and high-intensity endurance
                                                                                    exercise by 10%.1,10 As the body water deficit increases (ie, due to unreplaced fluid losses during outdoor competition,
                                                                                    training sessions, “making weight” in combat sports, or routine daily activities), both detrimental physiological effects
                                                                                    (ie, which often influence exercise) and clinical signs and symptoms proliferate.11–13
                                                                                        The following documented scenarios illustrate the wide range of fluid deficits that are experienced by athletes in
                                                                                    various team and individual sports. During hot summer months, collegiate American football linemen can lose 4–6 kg of
                                                                                    body water during a single summer practice session,5 and the sweat rates of tennis players and marathon runners during
                                                                                    competition reach extremes of 3.4 and 3.7 L/h, respectively.14,15 In moderate or cool environments, ultraendurance
                                                                                    athletes can experience extreme body water losses (7.8–8.5 kg, 11–12% of body mass) when competing in
                                                                                    a 12.3 h Ironman triathlon event.16 During 1.5–2.5 h training sessions across a variety of sports (eg, European soccer,
                                                                                    American football, tennis, cross country), body mass deficits typically range from 0.5–3.2% when fluids are readily
                                                                                    available.17–20 Other athletes purposefully dehydrate to qualify for lower weight classes (eg, wrestling, martial arts); this
                                                                                    regimen can result in body water losses of 3–5%.21,22 Even on days that are void of training or competition, it is possible
                                                                                    for healthy young adults to incur a 2.1% body mass loss during a single day of routine activities if no fluid is consumed.23

                                       At the opposite end of the hydration continuum, some endurance athletes consume a large volume of fluid that greatly
                                   exceeds the volume of fluid which he/she lost as sweat. Because sodium is lost in sweat, the outcomes are dilution of body
                                   fluids and reduced blood concentration of sodium.24 This phenomenon is appropriately named exertional hyponatremia or
                                   water intoxication. Not only does exertional hyponatremia degrade exercise performance (eg, due to undue fatigue), but severe
                                   cases may result in coma, pulmonary edema, cerebral edema, or death.4 The prominent signs and symptoms include dilute
                                   urine, swollen hands, disorientation, nausea, vomiting, skeletal muscle twitching, and grand mal seizure.25 Documented cases
                                   of symptomatic exertional hyponatremia26,27 have shown that fluid volumes of 10.3–14.7 L were consumed during exercise
                                   lasting 4–10 h. However, exertional hyponatremia has also been verified among non-endurance athletes,4,24 soldiers,28 and
                                   individuals who erroneously believed that excessive water intake was beneficial to performance or health.26 To reduce the risk
                                   of exertional hyponatremia, athletes are advised to gain no weight during exercise (ie, signifying fluid retention), and use
                                   a digital floor scale before and after exercise to confirm body weight change.3
                                       The aforementioned large range of body water changes, coupled with the dynamic/complex physiological effector
                                   responses that occur when the brain senses altered body water volume or concentration,29–33 represents great complexity
                                   that makes it difficult (ie, for clinicians, physiologists, athletes, or coaches) to accurately predict in advance the fluid
                                   deficit or excess which any athlete might experience during training or competition. This complexity explains, in part,
                                   why no single hydration biomarker allows a conclusive clinical diagnosis of dehydration for all athletes in all sport
                                   scenarios.34–39 Thus, we recommend creating an individualized hydration plan (IHP) for each athlete which incorporates
                                   multiple biomarkers, in agreement with numerous investigators and professional organizations.3,4,27,40–43 Specifically, we
                                   recommend three hydration indices which are inexpensive, valid, and require minimal technical expertise: body mass
                                   change, urine specific gravity, and rating of thirst. This approach provides athletes with data that is unique in the existing
                                   literature because most publications4,44–50 provide only a single hydration biomarker measurement (eg, urine specific
                                   gravity of 1.020) or a narrow range of values (eg, body mass loss of 3–4%) for all athletes, to indicate the threshold of
                                   dehydration’s detrimental effects. Using only one biomarker to assess hydration state is inferior, however, because (a)
                                   interindividual variability of fluid–electrolyte imbalances is large and is influenced by many factors;31,51–54 and (b)
                                   research studies31,55 have determined that combining two or three hydration indices (ie, body mass change, urine
                                   concentration, and thirst rating) improves the likelihood of distinguishing hypohydration from euhydration (ie, an optimal
                                   body water balance without underhydration or overhydration). In addition, our three criterion biomarker approach
                                   contributes importantly to the literature because no inventory of hydration biomarker data exists to guide interpretation
                                   of the unique body water changes (ie, deficits or excesses) which athletes experience in various sports.
                                       Therefore, the purpose of this review is to provide reference values for three field expedient biomarkers: body mass
                                   change, urine specific gravity, and rating of thirst. We have assembled a novel inventory of reference values for these
                                   three hydration biomarkers from field studies that involved outdoor competitions, training sessions, “making weight” in
                                   combat sports, and performing routine daily activities with no exercise. This collection of reference values is intended for
                                   use by clinicians, athletes, coaches, and physiologists, (a) as one of multiple resources that can be utilized to create and
                                   evaluate IHP for athletes and (b) to interpret hydration status before physical training or competition, post-exercise
                                   dehydration or excess fluid intake/retention, rehydration that optimizes recovery and health, and hydration status during
                                   routine daily activities.

                                   Search Methods
                                   Manual searches for relevant articles were performed using advanced search operators (eg, “and”, “or”, “not”). These
                                   searches focused on field studies that incorporated measurements of three human hydration biomarkers: body mass, urine
                                   specific gravity, and subjective ratings of thirst. Search inclusion criteria included English language, full-text, peer-
                                   reviewed articles with adult test participants, and availability through May 1, 2024. These searches were performed in the
                                   PubMed and Google Scholar databases; they employed numerous combinations of the following keywords, during
                                   separate explorations of the title/abstract and all text fields: “athlete”, “athletic”, “sports”, “hydration”, “hydrate”,
                                   “hydrated”, “hydrates”, “hydrating”, “biomarker”, “biomarkers”, “index”, “indexes”, “indices”, “indicators”, “urine
                                   specific gravity”, “thirst”, “body mass”, and “body weight”. These online searches acknowledged that the authors of
                                   hydration-relevant articles rarely distinguish the term “body mass” from “body weight”.

                                       Using these search terms within PubMed and Google Scholar databases, initially 3,224 articles were identified as
                                   potentially relevant (Figure 1). After duplicate records were removed, we reviewed titles and abstracts (ie, seeking
                                   studies that reported body mass change, urine specific gravity, and a subjective thirst rating as hydration indices) to
                                   identify potentially appropriate full-length articles which should be assessed further. Also, we performed manual searches
                                   of the reference lists in these relevant articles, as well as the bibliographies found in germane systematic reviews and
                                   meta-analyses. Finally, we investigated full text (.pdf) versions of 385 articles to ascertain if they met our inclusion
                                   criteria. Figure 1 illustrates the steps in this selection process.


                                   Results
                                   Using the keywords, inclusion criteria, and methods described above, we accepted 16 articles for analysis within the
                                   present review. All of these 16 articles measured body mass with a floor scale and urine specific gravity with a handheld
                                   refractometer; subjective ratings of thirst were measured using one of the two methods (eg, category scale or visual
                                   analog scale) described in footnotes b and e of Table 1. Thus, the following tables present measurements of only body
                                   weight change, urine specific gravity, and subjective rating of thirst during a variety of athletic and routine daily
                                   activities. For example, Table 1 presents reference values which can be utilized by clinicians, coaches, physiologists,
                                   and athletes to develop an IHP for use during outdoor athletic competitions and training sessions.
                                       Table 2 focuses on combat sport (ie, wrestling, boxing, judo) athletes who attempt rapid body mass loss to qualify for
                                   a weight class. Although our extensive literature search identified only a few studies of this type, values are provided for
                                   both pre- and post-weigh-in. Table 3 describes the changes of body mass, urine specific gravity, and subjective thirst ratings
                                   of two men who developed exertional hyponatremia during a 164-km summer ultraendurance cycling event.27 In column 4,
                                   mean (± SD) values are presented for a comparison group of 31 normonatremic cyclists who participated in the same event.
                                       In Table 1 and 2, the relationship between average body mass change and urine specific gravity (r = 0.50, p = 0.013), as well
                                   as the relationship between average body mass change and rating of thirst (r = 0.68, p = 0.001), were significantly correlated.
                                       Table 4 and 5 describe our three criterion hydration biomarkers, as they were measured during the routine daily
                                   activities of representative, healthy young adults. The test participants in these field studies23,68–70 were nonathletes who
                                   either performed recreational exercise (Table 4) or refrained from exercise (Table 5). The experimental design of the
                                   former study69,70 allowed a comparison of the average differences between morning and afternoon measurements. The

455	                                       Optimal IHPs incorporate biomarkers that are easy-to-use, field expedient, noninvasive, safe, portable, and
456	                                   inexpensive.3,4,30,34,75,77 In view of these criteria, several hydration biomarkers were initially considered for inclusion
457	                                   in the present review,34,37,39,84 including clinical assessment methods.35 The following five points influenced our decision
458	                                   to employ three hydration biomarkers: body mass change, urine specific gravity, and subjective rating of thirst. First, the
459	                                   2022 consensus statement of the International Olympic Committee Medical and Scientific Commission recommended
460	                                   that athletes monitor their body weight, urine specific gravity (or urine color), and thirst during periods of training or
461	                                   competing in hot environments.82 Second, an evaluation of 13 hydration assessment methods determined that body mass
462	                                   change, urine specific gravity, and rating of thirst were among the top five most suitable field techniques;34 the criteria for
463	                                   this finding were cost and time of analysis, technical expertise required, portability, and likelihood of an adverse event.
464	                                   Third, acute body mass change is recognized as the simplest and most accurate index of hydration status when serial
465	                                   measurements are collected in close proximity (eg, pre- and post-exercise, ≤ 4h) and when corrected for the mass of urine
466	                                   excreted and fluid consumed during the activity.4,34,85–88 Fourth, human body water balance primarily depends on two
467	                                   parameters: thirst that influences input, and urine excretion that determines output. When a deficit or excess of total body
468	                                   water exists, the kidneys act to restore euhydration. As a result, a change of urine concentration (eg, specific gravity) can
469	                                   distinguish a net loss or gain of body water (Figure 2), discriminate between euhydration and dehydration,4,27,89,90 and
470	                                   determine whether daily total water intake is adequate.68,91–93 Fifth, measurements of body mass, urine specific gravity,
471	                                   and thirst each have limitations when they are employed alone to assess hydration state, due to factors such as time
472	                                   of day, internal circadian rhythms, first morning hydration state, and dietary osmolar load.3,94–96 For example, consump­
473	                                   tion of a large bolus of water or a high protein diet may alter urine specific gravity acutely.30,97,98 Also, the intensity of
474	                                   thirst may be difficult to replicate consistently on a rating scale due to the interactions of numerous internal physiologic
475	                                   (eg, plasma osmolality and volume, oropharyngeal sensations) and external (eg, fluid characteristics, learned preferences,
476	                                   air temperature) influencing factors which are integrated by the brain.32,33,59,94–106 Therefore, we conclude that a single
477	                                   hydration assessment method (a) is not valid in all scenarios or for all individuals,34–39 and (b) does not provide
478	                                   unequivocal evidence of fluid intake inadequacy.31 However, research studies have shown that the combination of two
479	                                   hydration biomarkers makes identification of inadequate fluid intake or dehydration likely, and the combination of three
480	                                   indices makes this determination very likely.31,55,70
481	
482	                                   Hydration Biomarker Interrelationships
483	                                   Figure 2 provides a visual summary of body mass changes (%), subjective thirst ratings, and urine specific gravity values
484	                                   from 12 studies which focused on outdoor athletic competitions or training sessions (Table 1), and 24-h water restriction
485	                                   during routine daily activities (Table 5). All symbols represent group means (n = 6–28) and illustrate consistent
486	                                   agreement among these three hydration indices, in that all thirst ratings increased and all urine specific gravity values
487	                                   increased when a net body water loss occurred (ie, body mass decreased).
488	                                       Figure 3 illustrates the relationships of the three criterion biomarkers presented in Tables 1–5. The calculated
489	                                   Spearman’s rho correlation coefficients of these relationships (R2 = 0.41–0.88) are considered to be moderate (Panel
490	                                   C) and strong (panels A and B).107 Thus, we propose the following theoretical interpretation of Figure 3 that arises from
491	                                   widely recognized physiological responses. Specifically, both urine concentration within the kidneys (ie, represented here
492	                                   by increased specific gravity) and the sensation of thirst are strongly influenced by a body water deficit (ie, elevated
493	                                   extracellular fluid concentration). These effects are regulated by the release of vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) from
494	                                   the brain into the circulation,108–111 in response to increased plasma concentration, decreased plasma volume, and/or
495	                                   reduced arterial blood pressure.101,112 Additionally, thirst, urine concentration, and vasopressin release are influenced by
496	                                   oropharyngeal (ie, rear of the tongue, soft palate, and throat) nerve signals to the brain which rapidly reduce total fluid
497	                                   intake and modulate satiety,113,114 often before blood volume–concentration–pressure changes occur. We believe that
498	                                   these interrelated responses account for the strong correlation shown in Figure 3.
499	                                       Although an acute body mass change is recognized as the simplest and most accurate index of hydration status when
500	                                   serial measurements are collected in close proximity (as noted above), multiple factors influence the extent of this

515	                                   strong, respectively.107,117
516	                                       The findings described in the three previous paragraphs demonstrate that our three criterion hydration biomarkers
517	                                   responded consistently when a body water deficit occurred; this suggests satisfactory internal validity. Two individual
518	                                   exceptions to this observation appear in Table 3, in the form of cyclists who experienced exertional hyponatremia during
519	                                   a 164-km summer ultraendurance event. Row 1 of Table 3 shows that the comparison group with normal serum sodium
520	                                   levels (column 4) consumed an average of 5.9 L of fluid during 9.0 h of cycling. In contrast, the hyponatremic cyclists
521	                                   A and B consumed 13.7 L/8.9 h and 14.7 L/10.6 h, respectively, which resulted in serum sodium concentrations of
522	                                   130 mmol/L for both27 – well below the range observed among healthy adults (136–145 mmol/L).67 In terms of body
523	                                   mass, the comparison group lost 1.3%, cyclist A gained 4.3%, and cyclist B experienced virtually no change of body
524	                                   mass (+0.1%). This obvious difference among the two hyponatremic cyclists (ie, who had identical pre- and post-ride
525	                                   serum sodium values) likely resulted from a large difference in their sweat rates and the fact that cyclist B rode
526	                                   1.7 h longer than cyclist A. It is noteworthy that both cyclists A and B exhibited post-ride urine specific gravities and
527	                                   thirst ratings that were well below the mean values of the comparison group (column 4). This illustrates an important
528	                                   concept. Due to the complex interactions of many factors, some cases of exertional hyponatremia involve body mass gain
529	                                   (ie, overhydration and water retention that exceeds sweat, urine, and respiratory water losses),118,119 whereas other cases
530	                                   are associated with a large unreplaced sweat sodium loss and partially-replaced water loss.120–122 Thus, the development
531	                                   of exertional hyponatremia in cyclists A and B (Table 3) and the responses of hydration biomarkers were idiosyncratic.27
532	
533	                                   Considerations for Developing an IHP
534	                                   Previous publications describe (a) the negative effects which fluid–electrolyte imbalances can have on athletic perfor­
535	                                   mance, physiological functions, and health;3,4,46,51 and (b) the importance of developing an IHP for each athlete,123 as
536	                                   opposed to utilizing a single hydration biomarker value or a narrow range of values to indicate the threshold of
537	                                   detrimental effects for all athletes.84,98 In its simplest form, an IHP involves measuring an athlete’s sweat rate (described
538	                                   in the section titled “Body mass”) and planning the appropriate volume and timing of fluid intake in view of the
539	                                   anticipated rehydration opportunities of the sport. More sophisticated IHP models take into account an athlete’s tolerance
540	                                   to consuming a relatively large fluid volume,41 the concentration of electrolytes in sweat (ie, sodium, chloride,
541	                                   potassium),124,125 or the events that require sodium and carbohydrate in rehydration fluids.51,122,126 An IHP that
542	                                   incorporates most or all of these factors increases the likelihood that an athlete will attain the desirable middle ground
543	                                   between underhydration and overhydration, thereby optimizing performance.
544	
545	                                   Interpreting Biomarker Data
546	                                   The hydration biomarker data in Tables 1–5 are intended to be used concurrently with other information to interpret changes
547	                                   of hydration status. Because no single biomarker accurately indicates hydration status for all athletes, activities, and
548	                                   environments, and because different biomarkers sometimes provide conflicting information (ie, due to the dynamic
549	                                   complexity of human fluid–electrolyte regulation29–33), it is best to employ information from multiple sources to determine
550	                                   hydration status.31–55 One common technique involves comparing an athlete’s biomarker information to a single static
551	                                   value that represents the threshold of detrimental effects attributed to dehydration; in fact, most sport nutrition and human
552	                                   hydration publications4,44–50 provide a single biomarker value (eg, urine specific gravity of 1.020) or a narrow range of
553	                                   values (eg, body mass loss of 3–4%) for all athletes, activities, and environments. As a second source of information, each
554	                                   athlete can maintain a personal diary of body weight, urine specific gravity, and thirst measurements, before and after
555	                                   exercise; with this data, he/she can monitor trends across days and weeks to develop personalized reference values
556	                                   representing usual body weight changes, urine specific gravities, and thirst ratings. This diary of past hydration experiences
557	                                   can then be compared to each new competition or daily training session. The biomarker data of the present review
558	                                   represents a third source of information. Tables 1–5 provide activity-specific values which can be utilized by athletes,

569	                                   coaches, clinicians, and physiologists as one source of information to interpret IHP effectiveness. Changes (pre- versus
570	                                   post-exercise) of an athlete’s body mass, urine specific gravity, and thirst can be compared to the hydration biomarker
571	                                   averages in Tables 1–5, to determine if those changes are typical of that sport or activity; if dehydration, euhydration (ie,
572	                                   optimal body water balance), or overhydration exist; and the extent of body water loss or gain experienced (ie, departure
573	                                   from average values). Further, athletes and coaches who have not collected hydration biomarker data previously can refer to
574	                                   the values in Tables 1–5 for a general idea of what to expect when they begin measurements.
575	                                       With regard to the practical application of data in Tables 2–5, we offer four additional observations. First, the various
576	                                   methods of making weight in combat sports (Table 2) all result in dehydration and loss of body mass. Thus, during the process of
577	                                   restoring body mass to the pre-exercise level, we recommend that measurements of our three criterion biomarkers be scheduled
578	                                   throughout the refeeding and rehydration process. Second, in cases of overhydration (Table 3), changes of biomarker values may
579	                                   differ from one athlete to the next, depending on the volume and rate of fluid intake, sweat rate, body size, duration of exercise,
580	                                   and other factors.27 We recommend that a sports medicine physician be consulted if body mass increases and if urine specific
581	                                   gravity is unusually low post-exercise, suggesting retention of excess water; also refer to the section titled “Avoiding over­
582	                                   hydration”. Third, body mass tends to be lower in the morning, whereas first morning urine specific gravity and rating of thirst
583	                                   tend to be greater than midday and afternoon values, as shown in Table 4. If measurements are recorded at various times of
584	                                   the day, they may be confounded by water and food intake, voiding, exercise, and internal circadian rhythms.95 Thus, we
585	                                   recommend day-to-day consistency in the time of measurements.31,76 Fourth, as illustrated in Table 5, ordinary daily activities
586	                                   with no exercise can influence an athlete’s body water balance. To ensure that she/he begins a competitive event or daily training
587	                                   session well-hydrated, morning measurements of the three criterion variables should guide pre-exercise fluid intake.
588	                                       The following points present additional insights regarding the interpretation of biomarker data.
589	
590	                                        ● To discover an athlete’s typical patterns of fluid loss and fluid intake, several observations should be made in
591	                                          conjunction with training sessions and relevant field simulations of competitive events.
592	                                        ● Because our three criterion biomarkers reflect the responses of different organ systems, it is possible that one
593	                                          hydration index indicates a water excess whereas the other two indices suggest a water deficit. In this case, the
594	                                          majority indication should be utilized until another assessment is completed a few hours later.124
595	                                        ● When extreme or chronic biomarker changes are observed, consider possible causes and repeat measurements at
596	                                          regular intervals. If values do not return to pre-exercise levels within a reasonable time frame, consult a physician.
597

                                   inexpensive.3,4,30,34,75,77 In view of these criteria, several hydration biomarkers were initially considered for inclusion
                                   in the present review,34,37,39,84 including clinical assessment methods.35 The following five points influenced our decision
                                   to employ three hydration biomarkers: body mass change, urine specific gravity, and subjective rating of thirst. First, the
                                   2022 consensus statement of the International Olympic Committee Medical and Scientific Commission recommended
                                   that athletes monitor their body weight, urine specific gravity (or urine color), and thirst during periods of training or
                                   competing in hot environments.82 Second, an evaluation of 13 hydration assessment methods determined that body mass
                                   change, urine specific gravity, and rating of thirst were among the top five most suitable field techniques;34 the criteria for
                                   this finding were cost and time of analysis, technical expertise required, portability, and likelihood of an adverse event.
                                   Third, acute body mass change is recognized as the simplest and most accurate index of hydration status when serial
                                   measurements are collected in close proximity (eg, pre- and post-exercise, ≤ 4h) and when corrected for the mass of urine
                                   excreted and fluid consumed during the activity.4,34,85–88 Fourth, human body water balance primarily depends on two
                                   parameters: thirst that influences input, and urine excretion that determines output. When a deficit or excess of total body
                                   water exists, the kidneys act to restore euhydration. As a result, a change of urine concentration (eg, specific gravity) can
                                   distinguish a net loss or gain of body water (Figure 2), discriminate between euhydration and dehydration,4,27,89,90 and
                                   determine whether daily total water intake is adequate.68,91–93 Fifth, measurements of body mass, urine specific gravity,
                                   and thirst each have limitations when they are employed alone to assess hydration state, due to factors such as time
                                   of day, internal circadian rhythms, first morning hydration state, and dietary osmolar load.3,94–96 For example, consump­
                                   tion of a large bolus of water or a high protein diet may alter urine specific gravity acutely.30,97,98 Also, the intensity of
                                   thirst may be difficult to replicate consistently on a rating scale due to the interactions of numerous internal physiologic
                                   (eg, plasma osmolality and volume, oropharyngeal sensations) and external (eg, fluid characteristics, learned preferences,
                                   air temperature) influencing factors which are integrated by the brain.32,33,59,94–106 Therefore, we conclude that a single
                                   hydration assessment method (a) is not valid in all scenarios or for all individuals,34–39 and (b) does not provide
                                   unequivocal evidence of fluid intake inadequacy.31 However, research studies have shown that the combination of two
                                   hydration biomarkers makes identification of inadequate fluid intake or dehydration likely, and the combination of three
                                   indices makes this determination very likely.31,55,70

                                   Hydration Biomarker Interrelationships
                                   Figure 2 provides a visual summary of body mass changes (%), subjective thirst ratings, and urine specific gravity values
                                   from 12 studies which focused on outdoor athletic competitions or training sessions (Table 1), and 24-h water restriction
                                   during routine daily activities (Table 5). All symbols represent group means (n = 6–28) and illustrate consistent
                                   agreement among these three hydration indices, in that all thirst ratings increased and all urine specific gravity values
                                   increased when a net body water loss occurred (ie, body mass decreased).
                                       Figure 3 illustrates the relationships of the three criterion biomarkers presented in Tables 1–5. The calculated
                                   Spearman’s rho correlation coefficients of these relationships (R2 = 0.41–0.88) are considered to be moderate (Panel
                                   C) and strong (panels A and B).107 Thus, we propose the following theoretical interpretation of Figure 3 that arises from
                                   widely recognized physiological responses. Specifically, both urine concentration within the kidneys (ie, represented here
                                   by increased specific gravity) and the sensation of thirst are strongly influenced by a body water deficit (ie, elevated
                                   extracellular fluid concentration). These effects are regulated by the release of vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) from
                                   the brain into the circulation,108–111 in response to increased plasma concentration, decreased plasma volume, and/or
                                   reduced arterial blood pressure.101,112 Additionally, thirst, urine concentration, and vasopressin release are influenced by
                                   oropharyngeal (ie, rear of the tongue, soft palate, and throat) nerve signals to the brain which rapidly reduce total fluid
                                   intake and modulate satiety,113,114 often before blood volume–concentration–pressure changes occur. We believe that
                                   these interrelated responses account for the strong correlation shown in Figure 3.

                                   serial measurements are collected in close proximity (as noted above), multiple factors influence the extent of this

                                   Considerations for Developing an IHP
                                   Previous publications describe (a) the negative effects which fluid–electrolyte imbalances can have on athletic perfor­
                                   mance, physiological functions, and health;3,4,46,51 and (b) the importance of developing an IHP for each athlete,123 as
                                   opposed to utilizing a single hydration biomarker value or a narrow range of values to indicate the threshold of
                                   detrimental effects for all athletes.84,98 In its simplest form, an IHP involves measuring an athlete’s sweat rate (described
                                   in the section titled “Body mass”) and planning the appropriate volume and timing of fluid intake in view of the
                                   anticipated rehydration opportunities of the sport. More sophisticated IHP models take into account an athlete’s tolerance
                                   to consuming a relatively large fluid volume,41 the concentration of electrolytes in sweat (ie, sodium, chloride,
                                   potassium),124,125 or the events that require sodium and carbohydrate in rehydration fluids.51,122,126 An IHP that
                                   incorporates most or all of these factors increases the likelihood that an athlete will attain the desirable middle ground
                                   between underhydration and overhydration, thereby optimizing performance.

                                   Interpreting Biomarker Data
                                   The hydration biomarker data in Tables 1–5 are intended to be used concurrently with other information to interpret changes
                                   of hydration status. Because no single biomarker accurately indicates hydration status for all athletes, activities, and
                                   environments, and because different biomarkers sometimes provide conflicting information (ie, due to the dynamic
                                   complexity of human fluid–electrolyte regulation29–33), it is best to employ information from multiple sources to determine
                                   hydration status.31–55 One common technique involves comparing an athlete’s biomarker information to a single static
                                   value that represents the threshold of detrimental effects attributed to dehydration; in fact, most sport nutrition and human
                                   hydration publications4,44–50 provide a single biomarker value (eg, urine specific gravity of 1.020) or a narrow range of
                                   values (eg, body mass loss of 3–4%) for all athletes, activities, and environments. As a second source of information, each
                                   athlete can maintain a personal diary of body weight, urine specific gravity, and thirst measurements, before and after
                                   exercise; with this data, he/she can monitor trends across days and weeks to develop personalized reference values
                                   representing usual body weight changes, urine specific gravities, and thirst ratings. This diary of past hydration experiences
                                   can then be compared to each new competition or daily training session. The biomarker data of the present review
                                   represents a third source of information. Tables 1–5 provide activity-specific values which can be utilized by athletes,
